events.summary: September 2026 revenue was about NT$511.86bn (NT$511,857m), down 0.6% from August (NT$514,806m) and up 54.6% from September 2025 (NT$330,980m). January-September 2026 revenue was NT$3,898.73bn, up 41.1%. Released 13:30 Taipei on Thursday, which is 01:30 New York, before the US open. Q3 2026 revenue (July NT$467,580m + August NT$514,806m + September NT$511,857m) = NT$1,494.24bn: a record, up 17.62% from Q2 (NT$1,270.38bn) and up about 51% from Q3 2025 (NT$989.92bn). TSMC's Q3 guidance was US$44.6-45.8bn and assumed an exchange rate of 1 US dollar = 32 NT dollars, so the top of the range equals about NT$1,465.6bn (Focus Taiwan rounds it to about NT$1.47tn). At the guidance rate of NT$32, Q3 is about US$46.70bn: about 1.95% above the top of the range and 3.3% above its midpoint (US$45.2bn). At Thursday's Taipei closing rate of NT$31.875, it is about US$46.88bn. Media reported US$46.71bn. Q3 revenue was about 2.35% above the LSEG SmartEstimate of NT$1.46tn (19 analysts). TSMC will give its own US$ figure, at the quarter's actual average exchange rate, on 10-15 (not available yet). In US$ at NT$32, Q3 growth from Q3 2025 (US$33.10bn) is about 41% (a calculation).
events.why_it_matters: This is the fastest check on thesis pillars 1 and 2. Sales are still growing about 55% from a year earlier, and Q3 revenue landed above the top of TSMC's own range, so the AI-demand thesis got fresh support from TSMC's own numbers. The NT$ was slightly stronger than the NT$32 that guidance assumed (31.875 on Thursday), so the beat is not an artefact of a weaker currency. One small caution: September was the first month-on-month dip of the quarter (-0.6%). That is one month, while the thesis's early warning needs two months of falling sales. Focus Taiwan attributes the record quarter to AI-chip demand plus smartphone makers building inventory before new product launches.

events.summary: The Financial Times reported that OpenAI told investors its annualized revenue was about US$50bn at the end of September, about US$20bn below the roughly US$68bn figure that circulated in late September. The gap is reportedly a difference in counting method: Anthropic includes sales through cloud partners and OpenAI does not. OpenAI also reported 77% run-rate growth in Q3. AI and chip stocks fell: Nvidia -3%, AMD -4%, Broadcom -4%, Intel -5%, Oracle nearly -6%, CoreWeave nearly -8% (CNBC). The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 3.4% and the Nasdaq 100 1.4%, its worst day in seven weeks, as the report 'revived worries that the artificial-intelligence spending spree is becoming harder to justify' (Bloomberg). Bloomberg's pre-market story also cited a 'mounting energy shock' (oil rising on Middle East tension). A tier-3 market wrap adds rising bond yields and reports of Broadcom and Oracle arranging large financing for OpenAI. SMH fell 2.84% and TSM 3.01% (to $457.99, on 13.4m shares vs 7.3m on Wednesday).
events.why_it_matters: This explains most of Thursday's fall: the attribution puts -1.79 points on chips as a group and only -0.73 on TSMC itself (z -0.54, normal). OpenAI is one of the biggest end buyers of AI computing. If its revenue is lower than believed, investors worry about how long the chip spending that ends up as TSMC wafer orders can last. Nothing changed in TSMC's own reported numbers. It is a sentiment and expectations shock, not a TSMC fact.

events.type: contract / supply agreement (TSMC is the buyer)
events.summary: GlobalFoundries announced a US$2bn manufacturing agreement with an initial five-year term to make silicon interposers for TSMC's CoWoS advanced-packaging ecosystem at its Malta, New York fab. GF will expand capacity there and says this will be the first US-based source of silicon interposers, including embedded deep trench capacitor components. Volume production is expected to begin ramping in the first half of 2028. The release includes no TSMC quote, and TSMC's own newsroom has not published it.
events.why_it_matters: This adds a US supplier for one of the bottlenecks in making AI chips (CoWoS packaging) and extends TSMC's US manufacturing footprint, which can matter for US tariff policy (inference, medium). It is small in money terms. US$2bn over five years is roughly US$0.4bn a year if spread evenly (actual schedule not disclosed), a cost for TSMC rather than revenue, and under 1% of one quarter's revenue (Q3 about US$46.7bn).

why_chain.text: TSM fell 3.01% on Thursday 10-08 (to $457.99) and 1.02% on Friday 10-09 (to $453.31), -4.00% over the two days. Attribution: Thursday market -0.49, chips -1.79, TSMC -0.73 (z -0.54); two days market +0.20, chips -2.70, TSMC -1.50 (z -0.79). Mostly an industry move, and the company part is normal-sized.

Chip stocks fell as a group on Thursday: Philadelphia Semiconductor Index -3.4%, SMH -2.84%, Nvidia -3%, AMD -4%, Broadcom -4%, Intel -5%. TSM and SMH both gapped down at the open (TSM -1.25%, SMH -1.49%), so TSM moved with the sector.

The trigger was a Financial Times report that OpenAI's annualized revenue is about US$50bn, about US$20bn below the figure that had circulated, which 'revived worries that the artificial-intelligence spending spree is becoming harder to justify'. Rising oil (Middle East tension) added to the risk-off mood.

TSMC's own September/Q3 number was not the cause. It beat its guidance (about 2% above the top) and the LSEG consensus (about 2.35%), but analysts had already expected a result near the top of the range, so a beat was largely priced in and could not outweigh the sector selling.

Basic driver: chip stocks are priced on the expectation that AI companies' revenue will eventually justify their huge spending on chips. A lower-than-believed revenue figure at the most prominent AI company lowers confidence in how long that spending lasts. High-valuation stocks such as AI chipmakers fall first, even when today's sales are strong.
Friday: chips opened higher, then faded below Thursday's close while the S&P 500 rose 0.6%. No published reason was found. The likeliest explanation is a carry-over of Thursday's AI-spending worry.

products.name: CoWoS advanced packaging and silicon interposers (subject of the GlobalFoundries agreement)
products.what_it_is: CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) is TSMC's method of placing a large processor and its stacks of fast memory (HBM, high-bandwidth memory) side by side on a thin slab of silicon called an interposer, which wires them together into one package. GlobalFoundries will make some of those interposers for TSMC in New York.
products.analogy: The interposer is like a tiny motherboard made of silicon: a flat base with extremely fine wiring that lets the processor and its memory talk to each other almost as if they were one chip.
products.buyers: AI and high-performance computing chip designers whose multi-chip accelerators TSMC packages. The GF release names no end customers.
products.how_it_works: Silicon interposers 'sit under the compute logic and memory and provide a higher speed and lower power path for communications between the chips than would be possible using conventional organic packaging' (The Register, 2026-10-08). TSMC makes the processor die, then packages it with HBM on the interposer.
products.price: Not disclosed. The GF agreement is valued at US$2bn over an initial five-year term (GlobalFoundries, 2026-10-08), roughly US$0.4bn a year if spread evenly (calculation; actual schedule not disclosed).
products.sales: Not disclosed. TSMC does not report CoWoS or advanced-packaging revenue separately. Proxy (labelled): TSMC plans to spend 10-20% of its 2026 capex of US$60-64bn on 'high-end IC assembly and testing' (advanced packaging), roughly US$6-12.8bn (calculation from Focus Taiwan, 2026-07-16).
products.stage: CoWoS: shipping in volume from Taiwan (inference, high). GF Malta interposers: agreement signed 2026-10-08, with volume ramp expected in the first half of 2028.
products.size_for_company: The GF deal is a purchase by TSMC of about US$0.4bn a year on average, under 1% of one quarter's revenue (Q3 about US$46.7bn at NT$32). It matters strategically more than financially.
products.competition: Intel and Samsung offer rival advanced-packaging technologies, and outsourced assembly firms also package chips (general industry knowledge, not sourced in this run).
products.why_investors_care: Advanced-packaging capacity has been a limit on how many AI chips can be shipped. A second, US-based interposer source adds capacity and a US footprint relevant to tariff policy (inference, medium).
products.watch_next: CoWoS capacity and US packaging comments on the Q3 call (10-15). Any TSMC confirmation of the GF agreement.
